name: Chlorhexidine mouthwash
lead: Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic oral rinse, generally in the 0.05 to 0.2 percent range, used as an adjunct to toothbrushing to reduce dental plaque and gingivitis.[9] Chlorhexidine itself came into medical use in the 1950s and is on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List.[10]

Researchers describe it as one of the most studied antiplaque agents, and it has also been trialled in hospital settings, such as preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia and treating oral mucositis in cancer patients.[3][4][5][6] Known adverse effects include tooth staining, taste disturbance and, rarely, allergic reactions.[9][10] Its place in looksmaxxing discussion is mainly as a prescription or pharmacy rinse associated with gum and breath care.
infobox: Prescription or over the counter depending on country and strength

paras: Chlorhexidine rinses are used alongside normal tooth cleaning to reduce plaque and mild gingivitis; evidence is described as insufficient for moderate to severe gingivitis.[10] Reviews compare essential oil mouthwashes against it for plaque and gingival inflammation.[8]

Cochrane reviews examined oral hygiene care, including chlorhexidine rinses, for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia in critically ill patients.[3][6] A systematic review of basic oral care for oral mucositis in cancer patients and a 1994 randomised trial in radiation-induced mucositis also examined chlorhexidine rinses.[4][7] A New England Journal of Medicine trial assessed chlorhexidine as part of decolonisation of MRSA carriers.[5]

Extrinsic tooth staining appears after a month or more of use, and users may notice a bitter or altered taste.[10] Allergic reactions occur rarely, and the FDA label advises limiting use of the mouthwash to six months.[10]
Chlorhexidine is a cationic antiseptic that binds to oral surfaces and bacterial cell membranes. It reacts with anionic ingredients in some toothpastes, which can reduce its activity.[10]

A 2020 crossover study of 36 healthy adults found that seven days of chlorhexidine rinsing changed the salivary microbiome and some saliva and plasma markers compared with placebo.[1] A 2016 study reported reductions in salivary and plasma nitrite after nitrate intake with stronger mouthwashes.[2]

Human studies include crossover microbiome work in healthy volunteers, hospital trials for ventilator-associated pneumonia and mucositis, and a small report of salivary SARS-CoV-2 load after rinsing.[1][3][4][7][9] Findings vary by setting; the Cochrane reviews of oral care in intensive care are the main syntheses.[3][6]
Chlorhexidine rinses are mentioned in appearance-oriented oral care as a stronger antibacterial option, with staining of teeth the usual trade-off noted in clinical sources.[10]

card.summary: The reference antiplaque rinse; well studied for plaque, but staining and taste change come with it.
card.note: Tooth staining and altered taste with longer use; labels advise limited duration.

quick.overview:
Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic rinse used alongside brushing to cut plaque and mild gum inflammation. It is widely studied and is often the comparator in trials of other mouthwashes.

It is also used in hospital care, for example in oral care for ventilated patients and in cancer-related mouth sores.
quick.mechanism: It is a cationic antiseptic that binds to teeth, mucosa and bacterial membranes, giving a lingering antibacterial effect in the mouth.
quick.risks: Common effects are brown tooth staining after a month or more, taste disturbance and dry or irritated mouth; allergic reactions are rare. Labels advise limiting use of the mouthwash to about six months. A 2020 study found a week of use shifted the oral microbiome.
